title: The Google File System
abstract: A scalable distributed file system designed for large data-intensive applications. It explores fault tolerance, sequential access, and the trade-offs required when storage is built from commodity machines.

title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
abstract: A programming model and execution system for processing very large data sets with parallel operations across clusters. The abstraction hides scheduling, failures, and data distribution from the programmer.

title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
abstract: A distributed storage system for structured data that provides high availability and scalability. The design combines a sparse data model with a distributed file system and a coordination service.

title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
abstract: A highly available key-value storage system that uses partitioning, replication, and eventual consistency. It studies how large-scale services remain available during failures and network partitions.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally Distributed Database
abstract: A globally distributed database that combines transactions, strong consistency, and geographic scale. The system uses synchronized time and carefully designed replication to coordinate data across regions.

title: Ray: A Distributed Framework for Emerging AI Applications
abstract: A distributed framework for scaling machine learning and reinforcement learning applications. It provides a flexible programming model for stateful computation, scheduling, and fault-tolerant execution.

title: Okapi at TREC-3
abstract: An evaluation of probabilistic text retrieval methods and the Okapi system. It helped establish practical relevance ranking techniques for large document collections.

title: The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web
abstract: A link-analysis method that estimates the importance of web pages from the structure of hyperlinks. The approach connects graph centrality with information retrieval and search quality.

title: Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval
abstract: A machine learning perspective on ranking documents for search. It connects feature engineering, pairwise preferences, and evaluation metrics with practical information retrieval systems.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
abstract: A dense retrieval approach that represents questions and passages in a shared vector space. It demonstrates how learned representations can retrieve relevant passages without exact keyword overlap.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
abstract: A benchmark for evaluating information retrieval models across diverse domains and tasks. It makes it possible to compare lexical, dense, and hybrid retrieval methods under a common evaluation protocol.

title: Deep Learning
abstract: A broad foundation for representation learning with neural networks. It explains how multilayer models learn useful features for perception, language, and sequential data.

title: Attention Is All You Need
abstract: A sequence transduction architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms. The Transformer removes recurrence and convolution while improving parallelization and long-range dependency modeling.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
abstract: A language representation model that pre-trains bidirectional Transformer encoders on unlabeled text and adapts them to downstream language understanding tasks.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
abstract: A method that combines a parametric language model with a non-parametric dense index. Retrieved evidence can improve performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and make updates easier.

title: Efficient Transformers: A Survey
abstract: A survey of methods that reduce the computational and memory cost of Transformer models. It organizes sparse attention, low-rank approximations, and linear attention by their systems trade-offs.
